newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Amplats hit by weak results, outlook bleak.
newsitem.headline: Amplats hit by weak results, outlook bleak.

text.p: Shares in South Africa's Anglo American Platinum Corp (Amplats) dipped on Tuesday after it posted a weaker-than-expected set of half year results and warned on its full year earnings, dealers and analysts said.
By 0945 GMT Amplats stock had dropped 30 cents to 26.25 rand against a market trend that was sharply up. "It is reaction to the results," one dealer said.
On Monday the firm said its earnings per share for the six months to December 31 had fallen to 53.9 cents from 75.4 -- below analysts' expectations.
The firm slashed its dividend to 40.0 cents from 55.0 cents and warned that its full year earnings would also be down on last time.

The company blamed the poor performance on weak precious metal prices, higher working costs and a strike at its Rustenburg Platinum Holdings Ltd unit last June which cost the company around 250 million rand.
Amplats said it lost 100,000 ounces of platinum production as a results of the strike.
Rustenburg shares were also down and lost 50 cents to 61.50 rand.
South Africa produces 76 percent of the world's newly-mined platinum, of which about half comes from Amplats mines in the country's North West and Northern provinces.
Analysts said the outlook for the sector was bleak as precious metals prices were set to continue their current weakness.
The recent bull run by the rand would also hurt earnings as precious metals groups make their profits in U.S. dollars and have recently enjoyed a bout of rand weakness.
"The strength of the rand doesn't help at all. The stronger the rand, the less rand revenue these firms get," said Bruce Williamson, analyst at SBC Warburg.
Analysts said the results would also worry investors in South Africa's other main platinum firm, Impala Platinum Holdings Ltd.
But the firm's stock was holding up on Tuesday to post a 20 cents gain to 35.95 rand.

However, analysts said there were still areas of good news for the sector as firms in the industry generally have strong operations, excess capacity and good balance sheets when compared to fellow mining houses.

Another area of potential benefit is the news that Russia, the world's second largest producer of platinum, is known to have sold platinum, palladium and gold well above planned sales levels in 1995 and 1996, although the size of its stockpiles remain a closely guarded state secret.
If Russia sells out its stockpiles of platinum it could provide a huge boost to prices.
"The market has been waiting years for the Russians to run out of stock," one analyst said.
Analysts have previously estimated Russian platinum stockpiles at between two and five million ounces.
